My thoughts? "Ugh, this again." That is my thought on this.

I am not saying this is not bad, but the most important function of ICANN being given away - control of the DNS - is something that can be circumvented if enough people are pissed off. This is one reason why it's being given away in the first place - the ICANN DNS root only enjoys its position because of inertia and being relatively well-governed up to this point. If the US didn't give it away on their terms, other governments were going to make their own. This would have negative consequences across the Internet, in all likelihood - even though you might not connect to foreign web sites that you are aware of, a lot of infrastructures and organizations do, including some you almost certainly care about (goodbye Swiss VPN?), and would prevent foreign entities from connecting to our services, making certain freedom of speech goes bye bye elsewhere. There was talk with SOPA about replacing the ICANN DNS root with a peer-to-peer system, and you could start up your own root in your basement if you really wanted to. Other roots already exist, even if they're not used very much.

Furthermore, the US has not "owned" the Internet in probably a good 20 years, probably closer to 30. The Internet is a series of interconnected networks. The interconnects and the individual networks are largely owned by different organizations. While it is true that the US, at least through US-based corporations, owns a good chunk of the Internet, much of that is the domestic Internet. While the US has had significant guidance, it has grown less and less viable every passing year, and will eventually hit a thorough "so-what" level. It might already be there.

ICANN does have a few other things, most notably IANA, the agency that assigns IP address blocks, but since they gave away the last IPv4 block and are now only giving out IPv6 blocks, it's a lot less urgent than it used to be and they're a lot less powerful than they theoretically could be with IPv4.

Now, I am going to be blunt - this is not a good development, at all. It's been in the works for years. But this is far from the worst stuff that's coming down the pike Internet-wise. If you want to sharpen your pitchforks, sharpen it for TPP, whatever is going to be TISA's replacement, and all that other crap. Also save it for attacks against net neutrality and the cable companies dicking with the FCC, and while you're at it, sharpen a backup pitchfork for the continued erosion of privacy on the Internet, and that doesn't even begin to address the woes caused by elections being computerized.

This is bad, but the presentation is factually inaccurate (which leaves it open to undue ridicule, which weakens arguments against it), it might yet be stopped via court order at the last minute, and there are far bigger fish to fry. This can be managed. A lot of this other stuff, not so much.

The thing that most people don't realize is that this isn't necessarily an immediate thing. For example 15 (or so) years ago the major ISP's decided to implement a data cap. 250 gigs data caps 15 years ago was a non issue, since your average hard drive was 20 gigs and even the fastest connection was around 1 Mbps. But 15 years later, with all the online video games, streaming services, HD video, etc, 250 gigs ain't shit.

So the people who implemented those data caps saw what the future would be like, and planned against it. They claimed that only 1% of people were using that much data, and it was a non issue. But today, between youtube, netflix, and all the other shit, your regular Joe uses that much data no problem. And these data caps allow them to limit certain technologies, and progress. It allows them to maintain their monopoly.

Now apply this to what just happened. Is voat going to be taken down tomorrow? Probably not. But what about 15 years from now? What's going to be different then? We'll just have to wait and see.
